sections.category: AMD agrees to buy Taalas and says it intends to fold model-specific silicon into the Instinct roadmap

bullets.body: AMD announced on Thursday, August 6 that it has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Taalas, a Toronto company founded in 2023 that builds chips designed around one model rather than around a general instruction set. No price was disclosed, the deal is subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals, and no closing date was given, so nothing has changed in AMD's shipping line-up yet. Vamsi Boppana, AMD's senior vice president for the Artificial Intelligence Group, framed the purchase as adding differentiated inference performance and efficiency; AMD says it intends to fold the technology into its accelerator roadmap and build system-level products pairing it with Instinct GPUs, Helios rackscale systems, EPYC CPUs and ROCm. Ljubisa Bajic, Taalas co-founder and chief executive, said joining AMD gives the team scale, engineering resources and reach. The engineering argument sits in the manufacturing rather than the architecture: Taalas builds model-specific integrated circuits that embed a model's weights and dataflow into transistors instead of streaming them out of high-bandwidth memory, assembling a part of roughly 100 layers and customising only two metal layers per model, which it puts at a tape-out of about two months. Its HC1 test part, built on TSMC's 6-nanometer process, served Meta's Llama 3.1 8B at roughly 17,000 tokens per second. Taalas raised $169 million in February 2026 from Quiet Capital, Fidelity and Pierre Lamond, taking total funding to about $219 million. On the tape, AMD closed at $482.05 on Wednesday, August 5, down 7.04% for the session, then at $489.28 on Thursday, August 6, up 1.50%. The strategic read is that AMD has bought an answer to a question its GPU roadmap does not address: what a serving part looks like when the model is fixed and the only remaining variable is cost per token.

sections.category: Liquid AI ships a 2.6-billion-parameter agent model that runs in under 2.5 GB

bullets.body: Liquid AI published LFM2.5-2.6B on Tuesday, August 4: a 2.6-billion-parameter model pre-trained on roughly 34 trillion tokens, with the context window extended to 128K mid-training, aimed at agent work — planning, tool calls, multi-step tasks — that completes on the device instead of round-tripping to a hosted API. The footprint is the claim: under 2.5 GB of memory, with the company's own measurements at 220 tokens per second on an Apple M5 Max and 113 tokens per second on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, and close to 15,000 output tokens per second on a single NVIDIA H100 under high concurrency. On the ToolSandbox tool-use benchmark it reports 77.83, against 65.00 for Gemma 4 E4B-it and 52.40 for Gemma 4 E2B-it, and a Claw-Eval English average of 62.85; it also leads the models it was compared against on the IFBench, Multi-IF and IFStruct instruction-following suites. Runtime support at release covers llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang and ONNX, with transformers 5.0.0 or later. Every one of those figures is the vendor's own, published alongside the model rather than independently reproduced, so the honest reading is that the interesting number is the memory ceiling: a tool-calling agent loop that fits under 2.5 GB is deployable on hardware where a hosted-API dependency is the thing that cannot be shipped.

citations.label: Liquid AI on Hugging Face - Deploy local agents everywhere with LFM2.5-2.6B

sections.category: Meta ships a terminal coding agent in beta while a smaller one relicenses to sell the layer above it

bullets.body: Meta's research group published Muse Code and Muse Spark 1.2 on Wednesday, August 5. Muse Code is a terminal coding agent, explicitly in beta, installed on macOS and Linux by piping an install script from dev.meta.ai, and built to plan changes, write code and validate the result across large repositories while coordinating specialised subagents. Two design choices are worth lifting out for anyone building a comparable harness. The subagents are asynchronous and persist for the whole session rather than being spawned per task, and they decide when to report back to the main agent, which is what removes the round-trip latency from multi-step problems. And every model call, tool run, approval and edit is appended to a local event log, which Meta describes as making the agent replay-exact and restart-safe, so after a crash it resumes precisely where it stopped rather than re-deriving state from the working tree. Muse Spark 1.2 is the model underneath, a coding-focused update trained on more coding tasks with a wider spread of environments; the announcement names Terminal-Bench 2.1, DeepSWE 1.1 and Meta's internal coding benchmark as the comparisons but does not state the scores in the text. It is available now inside Muse Code and through the Meta Model API. The post says larger and more capable models are on the way, with no date attached to that.

citations.label: Meta Research - Introducing Muse Code and Muse Spark 1.2

bullets.body: At the other end of the size range, Herdr said on Thursday, August 6 that it has joined Y Combinator's F26 batch and, in the same post, relicensed its runtime from AGPL to Apache-2.0. Herdr is a terminal runtime for command-line coding agents: it organises them into panes, tabs and projects and keeps them running persistently on whichever machine it is installed on, including a remote host it installs itself onto over ssh, though the post is explicit that those machines are disconnected from each other today. No funding figure is given. The stated split is that the runtime people use today stays free under Apache-2.0 while commercial features are built on top, with multi-machine connectivity and clients beyond the terminal interface named as the two candidates. The licence change is the load-bearing part for anyone already embedding it. AGPL's network-use clause is what would have obliged a hosted service built on Herdr to publish its own source; Apache-2.0 removes that obligation, which both widens who can adopt the runtime and gives away the only thing that had reserved the hosted layer, leaving the paid tier it intends to sell defended by nothing but execution and being first.

citations.label: Herdr - Herdr is joining Y Combinator

sections.category: An experiment across more than 40,000 runs measures how well humans approve agent commands, and the answer scales with disguise

bullets.body: Alex Wauters published an analysis on the Scale X blog on Wednesday, August 5 of an interactive browser game in which the player is the human approver for a coding agent, accepting or denying each command under time pressure. Across more than 40,000 runs and roughly 409,000 approve-or-deny decisions, mean accuracy was 66.3%, and the miss rate tracked how much a hostile command looked like one: 11.7% for obviously destructive commands, 23.8% for persistent mutation attacks, 33.4% for exfiltration and code execution, and 35.0% for scope violations. 35.2% of players caught every threat, but only 20.8% managed that while blocking no more than one in five safe commands; 7% approved everything put in front of them; and 32.9% of sessions ended on a negative score. The single most-missed command was npm run analyze, approved 64.7% of the time even though the malicious payload was visible in the history log. The author is explicit about the artificiality — threats appeared in 34% of commands, far above any real workload, and a timed game is not a working day — and that caveat cuts both ways, because a real operator sees the hostile command far more rarely and is therefore less primed for it. What survives the caveat is the ordering: the further a hostile command sits from the shape people are trained to fear, the more reliably it gets waved through. That is an argument for putting the check in the tool layer, where the payload is inspected, rather than in the approval prompt, where only the command line is.

citations.label: Scale X - Humans missed 1 in 3 threats approving AI agent commands

sections.category: Cisco publishes twelve advisories and three identifiers land at 9.9

bullets.body: Cisco's product security incident response team published twelve advisories on Wednesday, August 5 — two critical, four high and six medium — covering Catalyst SD-WAN Software, IOS XE, IOS, the Integrated Management Controller, RoomOS and the Terminal Services Agent. The one to work first is the Catalyst SD-WAN security hardening release, which carries five identifiers: CVE-2026-20303, CVE-2026-20304 and CVE-2026-20310 at CVSS 9.9, CVE-2026-20312 at 8.8 and CVE-2026-20313 at 7.7. Cisco states these affect Catalyst SD-WAN Software regardless of device configuration, that there are no workarounds, and that it is not aware of any public announcements or malicious use of them. Fixed releases are 20.9.10, 20.12.8.1, 20.15.6, 20.18.4 and 26.1.2 depending on which branch a deployment sits on, against vulnerable trains running from before 20.9.1 through 20.18 plus release 26.1. The second critical advisory is the IOS XE security hardening release at CVSS 9.8. Two things distinguish this batch from the exploited-vulnerabilities feed that the same teams watch: these came out of internal testing rather than incident response, so the clock is set by disclosure rather than by observed attacks, and Cisco posted an advance notification on Wednesday, July 29 naming the publication date a week ahead, which means the maintenance window was schedulable rather than emergency.

sections.category: Unsloth stacks three package releases on Thursday after Tuesday's release made DSpark the default

bullets.body: Unsloth put three releases on PyPI on Thursday, August 6 — 2026.8.5, 2026.8.6 and 2026.8.7 — after 2026.8.3 on Tuesday and 2026.8.4 on Wednesday, five packages in three days. The changelog puts almost all of it under bug fixes: 2026.8.3 and 2026.8.6 are logged as fixes only, 2026.8.4 as training fixes, and 2026.8.5 adds Windows installation fixes. The one entry with shape to it is 2026.8.7, which lists DSpark support for DeepSeek-V4 Flash 0731 and a full rework of the training page. DSpark itself arrived earlier in the week, in the Studio release tagged v0.1.524-beta on Tuesday, August 4, where the release notes say DSpark is now on by default and describe it as doubling inference speed — without publishing a tokens-per-second figure on either side of that comparison, so the size of the gain cannot be checked from the project's own material. That same release shipped DeepSeek-V4 Flash 0731 quantisations ranging from 83 GB at UD-IQ1_S to 162 GB at UD-Q8_K_XL, support for Moonshot's Kimi K3 — a 2.8-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 104 billion active parameters, native vision and a one-million-token context window — and an automatic fallback from XET to plain HTTP when a download stalls, which is a continuation of the same download-reliability work logged against 2026.8.2. Read across the week, this is a maintenance cadence rather than a capability one: the training-page rework is the only change of shape a user would notice, and the rest is the project catching up with the models it added at the end of July.

sections.category: Bay Area / SV AI meet-up events

bullets.body: Las Vegas turns over today. Black Hat USA closes its six-day run at the Mandalay Bay Convention Center on Thursday, August 6, the second and last day of its two-day main conference; Ai4 at The Venetian and FMS: The Future of Memory and Storage at the Santa Clara Convention Center also close today, and BSides Las Vegas with its first dedicated AI-security track finished on Wednesday. What is left standing is DEF CON 34, which opens today at the LVCC West Hall and runs to Sunday, August 9. The way in now is $520 in cash at the door, the queue DEF CON calls LineCon; the badge is an open-source design built on bunnie Huang's Baochip and stays useful afterwards as an inspectable security platform. The AI Village sits in LVCC L1 W603 and runs HalCTF, an agentic security competition in which teams of up to five submit an agent as a container capped at 2.5 GB and point it at sandboxed targets. Thirteen models from 2.1B to 120B parameters are hosted centrally, so the entry cost is code rather than GPUs; scoring decays linearly as more teams solve a challenge, bonus points go to teams that win with smaller models, and first place takes a DGX Spark. If you are choosing between the two halves of the week, the AI Village is where the agent-security material actually is.

bullets.body: The nearest money deadline on this list falls tomorrow. SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit is at the Ritz-Carlton in Half Moon Bay on Tuesday, August 11 and Wednesday, August 12, and the full-experience pass is $1,895 through Friday, August 7, stepping to $2,195 from Saturday, August 8. It covers all sessions, the co-located CISO Forum Summer Summit, a welcome reception on Monday, August 10, a VIP dinner overlooking the bay on the Tuesday, breakfast, lunch and dinner across both days, fire-pit networking, post-conference materials and a discounted room rate subject to availability; the Golf Classic on Thursday, August 13 is a capacity-limited add-on. Two speaking deadlines fall this month for anyone who would rather present than pay: the AI Agent Security Summit takes submissions until Monday, August 17 for its London edition on Thursday, October 8, and until Friday, August 21 for New York on Wednesday, October 21. Talks must be strictly vendor-agnostic and built on original research, live demos or real case studies; selected speakers attend free with travel and up to two hotel nights covered. Those two remain the only editions listed as open. The separately-run AI Security Summit holds its San Francisco edition on Thursday, October 15 with a leadership track and a practitioner track. Colliding with that same Thursday is the San Francisco AI Engineering and Infrastructure Summit, which despite the name sits at the Crowne Plaza Palo Alto on El Camino Real, 8:30 AM to 3:30 PM, free, closed-door and practitioner-led with its speakers already set rather than an open call. Further out on the security track, SANS runs its AI Cybersecurity Summit on Monday, November 2 and Tuesday, November 3 at the Hilton Arlington Rosslyn in Arlington, Virginia, in person and live online, at $525 for the summit alone, with a $229 room rate that closes on Friday, October 9 and a refund cutoff of Wednesday, October 14; OWASP Global AppSec USA takes the Hyatt Regency San Francisco on Thursday, November 5 and Friday, November 6 with training the three days before; and the 19th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security meets on Sunday, November 15 in The Hague alongside ACM CCS, its paper deadline long closed.

bullets.body: On the silicon calendar, Hot Chips 2026 runs Sunday, August 23 to Tuesday, August 25 at Memorial Auditorium at Stanford in Palo Alto, hybrid, with live streaming, downloadable slides and Q&A for virtual attendees. Two deadlines are close: on-campus dorm housing must be booked by Sunday, August 16, and cancellations are honoured only to Wednesday, August 19. The Sunday is the tutorial day, a memory tutorial covering HBM evolution, 3D DRAM accelerators for generative inference and AI data demands, then a RISC-V tutorial on standards, adoption and enterprise use. Monday, August 24 carries CPU talks from IBM, Intel, NVIDIA, Fujitsu and Arm, a Waymo keynote on autonomous driving with an automotive session alongside it, and a GPU session from NVIDIA, AMD and Intel. Tuesday, August 25 carries an FPGA session from AMD — the one to watch if you are tracking the security-silicon intersection — a memory session with Samsung and XCENA, a networking session with Broadcom, NVIDIA and Mojo Vision, and accelerator talks from Meta, NVIDIA, Cerebras, Microsoft, SambaNova, Google and OpenAI. After that the infrastructure calendar runs: the AI Infra Summit at the Santa Clara Convention Center from Tuesday, September 15 to Thursday, September 17, five tracks across AI data centres, compute, data movement, data and models, and physical AI, with 8,000 attendees, 400 speakers and 250 partners expected across eight stages; the Edge AI and Vision Innovation Forum in San Jose on Wednesday, September 16; the OCP Global Summit at the San Jose McEnery Convention Center from Monday, October 12 to Thursday, October 15; NVIDIA's GTC Berlin from Tuesday, October 20 to Thursday, October 22, with GTC not returning to San Jose until March 2027; and SC26 in Chicago from Sunday, November 15 to Friday, November 20.

bullets.body: Ray Summit is at the San Francisco Marriott Marquis from Monday, August 24 to Wednesday, August 26 — a training day on the Monday, then two days of keynotes and breakouts — at $400 for the summit and $450 with training, with a five-pass bundle of the $450 tier promoted at $750 for all five against its $2,250 list price. The training day covers multimodal data processing, distributed foundation-model training and production inference in the morning, then physical AI, recommendation architectures and LLM deployment in the afternoon. The first vLLM Conference, hosted by Inferact, is co-located and every Ray Summit pass includes it across all three days. The ACM AI Leadership Summit is in Atlanta from Sunday, August 30 to Wednesday, September 2. Four San Francisco events still collide at the end of September. CoreWeave's Fully Connected is at Moscone South from Tuesday, September 29 to Thursday, October 1, with the $899 early-bird pass open through Saturday, August 29 and the $1,299 standard rate from Sunday, August 30; its three tracks cover building adaptive AI infrastructure, pushing models further, and evaluating and monitoring agents, with keynotes from CoreWeave's Mike Intrator, Peter Salanki, Chen Goldberg, Lukas Biewald and Shawn Lewis, NVIDIA's Ian Buck and Stanford's Fei-Fei Li, against 2,000-plus attendees, 30-plus breakouts and four-plus hands-on labs. The AI Conference runs the same window at Pier 48 Sheds A and B in Mission Rock, five tracks across AI frontiers, AI builders, the AI stack, applied AI and AI strategy, with 5,500 attendees and 120-plus speakers expected including Peter Norvig of Stanford HAI and Emmanuel Ameisen of Anthropic; its September 29 workshop-and-hack day is sold out at 350 seats, and the two-day pass for September 30 and October 1 is still open. OpenAI's DevDay is at Fort Mason on Tuesday, September 29 with applications already closed, and Newcomer's Machine Earning AI Summit is in San Francisco the same day. After that: the Runway AI Summit on Wednesday, September 30; World Summit AI in Amsterdam on Wednesday, October 7 and Thursday, October 8; the PyTorch Conference in San Jose on Tuesday, October 20 and Wednesday, October 21; AGNTCon and MCPCon North America at the San Jose McEnery Convention Center on Thursday, October 22 and Friday, October 23; GitHub Universe at Fort Mason on Wednesday, October 28 and Thursday, October 29; the application-only AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco from Wednesday, November 11 to Friday, November 13; Newcomer's Cerebral Valley AI Summit on Thursday, November 12; AWS re:Invent from Monday, November 30 to Friday, December 4; NeurIPS in December; and The AI Summit New York on Wednesday, December 9 and Thursday, December 10.

bullets.body: On the robotics calendar, IEEE-RAS Humanoids 2026 has closed every submission window and is now purely a decision calendar: competition notifications on Monday, September 21, workshop and tutorial notifications on Monday, September 28, paper notifications on Tuesday, October 6, early-bird registration on Friday, October 16 and camera-ready papers on Monday, October 26, before the conference itself at the Santa Clara Convention Center from Sunday, December 6 to Wednesday, December 9. On AI Tinkerers, the local picture improved today: Palo Alto on Tuesday, August 18, 6:30 to 9 PM PDT, has moved onto the global calendar as a listed session rather than the unverified chapter page it was, and two more entries joined the same Tuesday — Manchester, New Hampshire, 5:30 to 7:45 PM EDT, and a Seattle Women in AI builders track, 5 to 8 PM PDT, with lightning demos and code audits. August 18 is now the calendar's last dated entry. Tonight's session is the Los Angeles builder meetup and live demos, Thursday, August 6, 6 to 8 PM PDT, which has already rolled off the calendar's forward list because it starts today. Between here and there: the New York Vision Hack v.2 with Google Cloud and Roboflow tomorrow, Friday, August 7, 4 to 10 PM EDT; the Mombasa chapter launch on edge AI, local small models and autonomous swarms, 9 AM to noon EAT, and a Dubai demo day, 11:30 AM to 3 PM local, both on Saturday, August 8. A five-city Tuesday follows on August 11 — a Valencia go-to-market teardown 6 to 9 PM CEST, an Upstate New York build night 6 to 8:30 PM EDT, Houston on agentic workflows 5:30 to 8 PM CDT, Chicago with Cloudflare and PostHog 5:30 to 8 PM CDT, and a Seattle AI-and-biology demo night with NVIDIA and the Allen Institute 6 to 9 PM PDT. Then Wednesday, August 12 brings a Valencia rooftop founders' night, Brussels on the agentic software lifecycle 6:30 to 9:30 PM CEST and Raleigh 5:30 to 7:30 PM EDT; Atlanta at ATL Tech Week on Thursday, August 13, 1:45 to 3:45 PM EDT; Bremen on Friday, August 14, 6 PM CEST; and on Saturday, August 15 the inaugural Da Nang meetup 9 AM to noon local, an Islamabad and Rawalpindi session 2 to 5 PM PKT and a Riyadh Claude Code workshop 1:30 to 4:30 PM local. Sunday, August 16 is the London Agents vs Wall Street hackathon, 9 AM to 8 PM BST. The Medellin session the calendar previously held for August 7 no longer appears and should be treated as unscheduled, and nothing is dated in San Francisco, San Jose or Pleasanton.
